teaser.text: Cisco sells the systems that let organizations connect, protect and understand their technology. Its business combines equipment sales with recurring software, support and services, so following a dollar means following both the installation and the years after it.

stock.title: Cisco stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Cisco's forecast shows weighted scenarios, key AI-driven risks, real free cash flow, and the valuation investors pay today.
stock.opening: Cisco's weighted forecast moves from $117.88 today to $105.81 by October 2029, a 6% loss including dividends. Cisco's AI opportunity matters only if orders become profitable shipments, cash and durable software growth.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Cisco's business, its rivals, its management, and its risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Cisco's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: Cisco’s weighted forecast points to a lower share price by October 2029, because the 6% loss including dividends hinges on AI orders becoming profitable revenue and cash. The weighted price moves from $117.88 today to $105.81 by October 2029.

The bear case reaches $67.43 with 30% probability. The base case carries 50% probability. The bull case reaches $159.44 with 20% probability. The base case assumes earnings growth alongside a P/E decline from 25x to 23x by October 2029.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Cisco's stock forecast?

paragraphs.text: In October 2026, Supermicro systems become orderable through Cisco’s partners. Completed installations and shorter delivery waits would test supply relief. On November 12, Cisco reports Q1 FY2027, with an adjusted gross-margin target of 65.0–66.0%. Through FY2027 and FY2028, broader AI demand, campus refreshes, software renewals and Splunk cross-selling support the bull case; delayed installations, rising inventory and weaker cash conversion support the bear case.
Cisco’s AI opportunity matters only if orders become profitable shipments, cash and durable software growth.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Cisco really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow subtracts capital spending from operating cash flow. Cisco generated $12,767 million after spending $1,410 million on capital projects. Capital spending rose while operating cash flow stayed flat, so less cash remained after investment. The measure also has limits: research and development is expensed, while outside manufacturing costs run through operating cash flow.

dividend.title: Cisco dividend
dividend.meta_description: Cisco's dividend rose steadily, while cash flow covered dividends but not all shareholder returns after stock pay.
dividend.opening: Cisco's dividends rose by 0.04 per share each year from FY2022 through FY2026, reaching 1.68 per share in 2029 in the base case. Cisco generated $12.767 billion of free cash flow and paid $6.553 billion in dividends, but real free cash flow after stock pay was $8,937 million, so dividends and buybacks exceeded it.
dividend.closing: The full memo also answers how Cisco's business works, how its rivals compare, how Cisco's management allocates capital, and what risks could change the outlook.

blocks.heading: How much does Cisco pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The dividend path follows Cisco's record but recognizes its cash constraints. Dividends rose by 0.04 per share each year from FY2022 through FY2026. The base case continues that pattern, reaching 1.78 per share in 2029. The bear case freezes the annualized rate at 1.68, while the bull case reaches 1.88 as AI deliveries improve cash conversion.

blocks.heading: Does Cisco's dividend fit its cash flow?

paragraphs.text: Stock compensation makes the shareholder test stricter. The cash-flow statement adds this noncash expense back, so conventional free cash flow includes it. Subtracting $3,830 million produces “real free cash flow” of $8,937 million. This is an economic allowance for employee ownership, not a second cash payment. Buybacks and this allowance should not both be deducted as though they were identical costs.

Free cash flow is operating cash left after necessary capital spending. Cisco generated $14.177 billion from operations and spent $1.410 billion on property and equipment, leaving $12.767 billion of free cash flow. It paid $6.553 billion in dividends and repurchased $6.106 billion of stock, leaving little cash for growth that requires more inventory or supplier prepayments.

blocks.heading: What has Cisco guided for fiscal 2027?

paragraphs.text: Cisco’s fiscal year ends in July rather than December, so fiscal 2027 covers the twelve months leading up to July 2027. Management’s August guidance calls for revenue of $72.2–$73.4 billion and adjusted earnings of $5.05–$5.11 per share. For the first quarter, it expects revenue of $18.0–$18.2 billion.

Adjusted earnings are a comparison measure, while GAAP earnings follow standard accounting rules. Cisco’s GAAP forecast is $4.00–$4.06 per share because it includes stock compensation, acquisition-related amortization and restructuring charges. Stock compensation can dilute owners, and acquisitions and restructuring still cost money, so investors must compare like with like.

blocks.heading: Did Cisco keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Cisco did meet important stated promises. It forecast up to US$60.0 billion of fiscal 2026 revenue and delivered US$63.3 billion. It also returned 94% of free cash flow against a policy minimum of 50%. Free cash flow is the cash left after operating and investment needs; it can be returned through dividends or buybacks. But cash returned is not the same as ownership preserved if stock awards keep issuing claims on the company.

blocks.heading: How have Cisco revenue and profit trended?

paragraphs.text: Hyperscalers, the large cloud operators building AI infrastructure, supplied about 6% of fiscal 2026 sales. Their purchases can be large and uneven, so orders must be followed through shipments and collections. Diluted EPS rose to $3.33, while the diluted share count fell only 0.3%; buybacks therefore contributed little. The repeatability test is whether equipment, recurring contracts and cash collections improve together.

Gross margin shows what remains after the direct cost of providing Cisco’s products and services. It fell from 64.9% to 64.5%, as the mix shifted toward Networking and memory became more expensive. Pricing and productivity partly offset that pressure. Operating margin improved from 20.8% to 24.3% because sales grew faster than the overall operating-cost base. That is operating leverage, not proof that every product became more profitable.
